Empirical Research Plan  
“Compulsory Schooling and Labor-Market Outcomes in Germany”

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Two–stage Difference-in-Differences (DiD) / Instrumental-Variables (IV) design that exploits the staggered increases in the minimum school-leaving age (MSLA) across West-German Länder during the 1950s–1970s.

• First stage (policy effect on schooling):  
  Schooling_it = α + β ReformExposure_is + γ_i + δ_s + ε_it.  
• Second stage (causal effect on outcomes):  
  Outcome_it = α + ρ ĴSchooling_it + γ_i + δ_s + υ_it,  
  where ĴSchooling is the fitted value from stage 1 (i.e., years of compulsory schooling induced solely by the reform).

Why appropriate  
– Reform implementation dates were decided by state education ministries for administrative reasons and are widely viewed as unrelated to contemporaneous local labor-market conditions for unborn cohorts.  
– Staggered timing yields quasi-experimental variation that can be exploited with modern DiD estimators or with an IV that maps policy exposure into extra schooling.  
– Long GSOEP panel lets us observe entire earnings histories of affected and unaffected cohorts.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
ReformExposure_is = 1 if individual i, born in year b in state s, had not yet reached the pre-reform leaving age when state s raised the MSLA. In practice:

 treated if  birthyear b  ≥  (ReformYear_s  –  PreReformMSLA)

Control group  
Individuals born in the same state but just old enough to fall under the old MSLA form the within-state controls. Additional controls come from states that had not yet reformed in the same birth years (staggered adoption).

Treatment timing / key variation  
West-German Länder raised the MSLA from 8 to 9 years between 1949 and 1969 (Hamburg 1949, Bavaria 1969, etc.). Hence treatment is cohort-by-state specific and effectively “one-shot”.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Parallel trends (DiD): In the absence of the reform, labor-market outcomes of near-adjacent birth cohorts in the same state would have evolved similarly.  
 • Plausibility: Birth-year differences of at most two years fall in the same macro cycle, and state fixed effects soak up level differences.

A2 No other cohort-specific shocks coincide systematically with reform timing.  
 • Plausibility: The education reforms were not accompanied by state-specific labor-market programs targeted only at the treated cohorts.

A3 Exclusion restriction (IV): The reform affects adult earnings solely through additional schooling, not via, e.g., curriculum changes.  
 • Plausibility: Historical documents show that curricula changed nationally, not differentially with reform timing, but still needs to be tested (see threats).

A4 Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One individual’s treatment status does not affect another’s outcome.  
 • Plausible because additional schooling of one cohort is unlikely to meaningfully alter labor-market conditions decades later for the comparison cohort.

A5 First-stage relevance: ReformExposure significantly increases years of schooling.  
 • Documented in earlier descriptive work and easy to verify in GSOEP.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Migration across Länder before school start  
 • Remedy: Assign treatment using state of residence at age 10 (available in retrospective GSOEP questions) rather than current residence. Run robustness dropping movers.

T2 Concurrent changes in vocational-training regulation  
 • Remedy: Control for indicators of state-level vocational training reforms; run event-study graphs to show no pre-trends.

T3 Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in two-way-FE DiD  
 • Remedy: Implement Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) group-specific ATT estimator or Sun-Abraham (2021) event-study to avoid negative weighting issues.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)          # fast fixed-effects OLS / IV
library(did)             # Callaway & Sant'Anna estimator
library(lmtest)          # coeftest for cluster-robust SE
library(sandwich)

# ---- 1. Data loading ----
gsoep  <- read_csv("gsoep_long.csv")            # individual x year
reform <- read_csv("msla_reform_years.csv")     # state-level table: state, reform_year

# ---- 2. Variable construction ----
df <- gsoep %>% 
  mutate(birth_year    = year(birth_date),
         age           = survey_year - birth_year) %>%
  left_join(reform, by = "state") %>%
  # exposure: 1 if individual had not yet reached old MSLA when reform occurred
  mutate(exposure  = ifelse(birth_year >= (reform_year - 14), 1, 0),  # 14 = 8 yrs school + 6 age at start
         post      = ifelse(survey_year >= reform_year, 1, 0),
         treat_cohort = exposure) %>% 
  # keep cohorts born ±8 yrs around each reform
  filter(birth_year >= reform_year - 20,
         birth_year <= reform_year + 5) %>%
  # outcome variables
  mutate(ln_earnings = log(real_monthly_earnings),
         employed    = as.integer(employment_status == "employed"))

# ---- 3. First stage (reform -> schooling) ----
fs <- feols(years_schooling ~ exposure | state + birth_year, 
            cluster = "state", data = df)
summary(fs)

# ---- 4. 2SLS (schooling -> earnings) ----
iv <- feols(ln_earnings ~ 1 | state + birth_year | years_schooling ~ exposure, 
            cluster = "state", data = df)
summary(iv)

# ---- 5. Modern DiD ATT (robust to staggered timing) ----
cs <- att_gt(yname = "ln_earnings",
             gname = "reform_year",        # timing group
             idname = "id",
             tname = "survey_year",
             xformla = ~0,                 # no covariates
             data = df,
             panel = TRUE)
overall_att <- aggte(cs, type = "simple")
summary(overall_att)

# ---- 6. Robustness: drop internal migrants ----
nomovers <- df %>% filter(moved_state_before_16 == 0)
iv_nomovers <- feols(ln_earnings ~ 1 | state + birth_year | years_schooling ~ exposure,
                     cluster = "state", data = nomovers)
summary(iv_nomovers)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (human-capital) predicts a positive effect: an extra year of schooling should raise wages by 5-10 %. Historical German estimates cluster around 6–8 %. Given that the MSLA reform added roughly 0.8–1.0 years of education on average (β̂₁ in first stage), I expect ρ ≈ 0.06–0.08 in log earnings terms, i.e., 6–8 % higher wages for the compliers. Employment probability effects should be positive but smaller (≈1–2 ppt).

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
----------------------------------------------------------------
Criterion (1 = satisfied, 0 = doubtful)

1. Strong first stage (F>10) ................. 1  
2. Parallel trends (visual & placebo tested) .. 0.8  
3. No endogenous migration .................... 0.8  
4. Exclusion restriction (no other channels) .. 0.6  
5. Robust to heterogeneous timing estimators .. 1  

Overall: 4.2 / 5 — credible but exclusion restriction needs most scrutiny.
